query: What signals suggest an incident will take longer to resolve?

per_column.name: resolution_hours
per_column.rationale: This is the target/outcome measure derived from opened_at and closed_at timestamps, directly capturing how long an incident takes to resolve. Central to the query. Values are consistent with the timestamp fields present. NULLs for unclosed incidents are correct behaviour.

per_column.name: resolution_hours.1
per_column.rationale: An exact duplicate of resolution_hours (identical value distribution). Adds no new analytical axis; trivially redundant. Grounding is fine but usefulness is near zero as a restatement.

per_column.name: priority_level
per_column.rationale: Priority is a plausible signal for resolution time, but this is essentially a numeric restatement of the existing 'priority' original column, offering limited new leverage. Values appear grounded in the priority field.

per_column.name: is_critical_high
per_column.rationale: A binary flag derived from priority. Grounded, but largely redundant with priority_level and heavily skewed (459 vs 41), giving weak discriminating power. A bare threshold flag over an existing field.

per_column.name: category_complexity
per_column.rationale: Mapping category to an ordinal complexity score gives a genuine new axis relevant to resolution time. However the complexity ranking is an imposed heuristic not directly stated by the text; the assignment (e.g. database=3, VPN/WiFi=2) is a warranted but partly subjective inference.

per_column.name: same_assignee_caller
per_column.rationale: Constant value 0 across all 500 rows. Near-constant columns provide no analytical leverage. Grounded but useless for grouping or modelling.

per_column.name: updater_is_system
per_column.rationale: Whether the updater is a system account is a plausible, non-trivial signal derivable from sys_updated_by. Reasonable split (336/164). Grounding depends on correctly recognising system accounts, a warranted inference.

per_column.name: status_risk
per_column.rationale: An ordinal risk derived from state gives some analytical leverage for resolution likelihood/time. However the mapping from state to a risk score is an imposed heuristic and somewhat redundant with the existing state column.

per_column.name: time_risk
per_column.rationale: Appears to be a bucketing of resolution time / elapsed time into a risk band. If derived from resolution_hours it is circular with the outcome and leaks the target, reducing usefulness. Mapping basis is not clearly warranted from source; samples show inconsistent relation to resolution_hours.

per_column.name: description_complexity
per_column.rationale: A complexity proxy from short_description; risks being a mere text-length/token-count restatement (binary 1/2 split resembles a length threshold), which the rubric flags as low-leverage. Grounded as a reading of the text but weak analytical value.

judge.rationale: The set contains one strongly useful, well-grounded outcome measure (resolution_hours) plus several plausible signals (category_complexity, updater_is_system, priority_level, status_risk) that give some new axes for analysing resolution time. However usefulness is dragged down by an exact duplicate (resolution_hours.1), a fully constant column (same_assignee_caller), redundant priority restatements, and generic length-like proxies (description_complexity). time_risk risks leaking the target. Grounding is generally acceptable: values are sound readings of timestamp, priority, state, category and updater fields, with correct NULLs for unresolved incidents; some columns rely on imposed heuristic mappings that are warranted but subjective. No clear hallucinated facts observed.
